c.tagline: Ancient shogunate capital of temples, the Great Buddha, and seaside calm

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are reliable, spotlessly clean, and metered with no need to tip; rear doors open automatically

emergency.note: Dial 110 for police, 119 for ambulance/fire; English support is available via the Japan Visitor Hotline 050-3816-2787

avoid.reason: Weekend crowds on Komachi-dori and the packed Enoden line invite rare pickpocketing, and black kites snatch food from hands at the beaches.

hood_desc: The bustling heart of the city and main arrival point by train, with the pedestrian shopping street Komachi-dori packed with souvenir shops and street food leading toward Tsurugaoka Hachimangu Shrine.

Home to Kamakura's most famous sight, the towering bronze Great Buddha at Kotoku-in, as well as Hase-dera Temple with its hillside gardens and ocean views, a short ride from the station on the Enoden line.
A tranquil, forested area north of the station dotted with major Zen temples like Engaku-ji and Kencho-ji, popular for quiet contemplative walks especially during autumn foliage.
A laid-back residential beach neighborhood east of Yuigahama, quieter than its neighbor, with a family-friendly stretch of sand and views toward the Miura Peninsula.
Kamakura's main beach district, lined with surf shops and casual cafes, drawing a younger, laid-back crowd especially in the warmer months.

water.note: Tap water is safe to drink everywhere.

transit.pay: IC cards (Suica/Pasmo) tap-in tap-out, or single tickets
transit.note: The scenic Enoden tram connects Kamakura Station to Hase, Yuigahama, and Enoshima; JR trains link Kamakura directly to Tokyo and Yokohama

train: JR Yokosuka Line direct to Tokyo (~1 hour) and Yokohama (~25 min)
bus: Airport limousine buses run from Haneda/Narita to nearby Yokohama, then onward by train

tip.s: not customary, can be considered rude
tip.r: Tipping is not expected anywhere in Japan, including restaurants, taxis, and hotels; excellent service is standard and included

food.name: Shirasu-don
food.desc: Sagami Bay whitebait heaped over rice, served either raw and translucent or briefly boiled; the signature bowl of the Shonan coast.

places.name: Akimoto
places.note: Local benchmark for generous raw shirasu bowls; raw stock often sells out.

places.name: Tobiccho
places.note: Whitebait specialist offering raw, boiled and marinated versions on one bowl.

places.name: Shirasuya
places.note: Fisherman-run shop by the Enoden line, as fresh as shirasu gets.

food.name: Kamakura vegetables
food.desc: Kamakura-yasai are heirloom and Western vegetables grown on small local farms, prized by Tokyo chefs and served barely dressed.

places.name: Kamakura Renbai farmers market
places.note: Growers' market running since 1928; buy straight from the farmer.

places.name: Magokoro
places.note: Long-running vegan cafe building its plates around local produce.

food.name: Shojin ryori
food.desc: Zen temple cuisine of tofu, sesame, mountain vegetables and clear broths, a legacy of Kamakura's great monasteries.

places.name: Hachinoki Kita-Kamakura Honten
places.note: Beside Kenchoji temple; refined multi-course vegetarian, reserve ahead.

places.name: Kaiko-an at Hasedera
places.note: Temple cafe with vegetarian curry and a view over the bay.

food.name: Kenchin-jiru
food.desc: A hearty clear soup of root vegetables, konnyaku and crumbled tofu said to have been born at Kamakura's Kenchoji temple.

places.name: Kenchoji temple precinct
places.note: The dish takes its name from this temple; nearby shops serve it year round.

places.name: Komachi-dori soba shops
places.note: Most noodle houses offer kenchin soba or udon in cooler months.

food.name: Hato Sabure
food.desc: Buttery dove-shaped shortbread biscuits, made in Kamakura since 1894 and the town's most-carried edible souvenir.

places.name: Toshimaya Honten
places.note: The original bakery; the flagship store sells tins and single warm biscuits.

places.name: Toshimaya Komachi branch
places.note: Handier for a quick stop on the walk up from the station.

food.name: Kamakura ham
food.desc: Cured hams and sausages made locally since 1900, eaten in sandwiches and croquettes along the shopping street.

places.name: Kamakura Ham Tomioka Shokai
places.note: Founding maker; sells sandwiches and cutlets alongside gift packs.

places.name: Komachi-dori food stalls
places.note: Croquette and sausage counters line the street; eat as you walk.

food.name: Matcha at a temple teahouse
food.desc: Whisked bowls of matcha served with a seasonal sweet in temple gardens, a habit Kamakura has kept since its Zen heyday.

places.name: Kyukoan at Hokokuji
places.note: Drink matcha looking into the famous bamboo grove; small extra fee.

places.name: Kisen-an at Jomyoji
places.note: Tatami teahouse above a dry landscape garden, usually far quieter.

places.name: Sasa no Ha
places.note: Sweets shop pairing matcha with warabi mochi and seasonal wagashi.

food.name: Shonan craft beer
food.desc: The Shonan coast brews its own ales and wheat beers, poured in Kamakura's small bars and often drunk within sight of the sea.

places.name: Yorozuya Honten
places.note: Standing bar with a rotating tap list of Kamakura and Shonan beers.

places.name: Komachi-dori beer stands
places.note: Several shops pour local Kamakura Beer by the cup to take away.

landmarks: Great Buddha of Kamakura (Kōtoku-in)
A serene 13-meter bronze Amida Buddha cast in 1252 has meditated in the open air for centuries after tsunamis swept away its hall.
Tsurugaoka Hachimangū Shrine
Kamakura's grand Shinto shrine, founded by the Minamoto shoguns, crowns a broad ceremonial avenue of torii gates and cherry trees from the beach.
Hase-dera Temple
A hillside temple famed for its nine-meter gilded eleven-headed Kannon, hydrangea-lined paths and sweeping views over Sagami Bay.
Hōkoku-ji Temple (Bamboo Temple)
A small Zen temple whose grove of nearly 2,000 moso bamboo stalks filters green light onto a teahouse serving matcha in the hush.
Kenchō-ji Temple
Japan's oldest Zen training monastery, founded in 1253, ranks first among Kamakura's Five Great Zen Temples with towering gates and ancient junipers.
Engaku-ji Temple
A vast Zen complex tumbling down a wooded Kita-Kamakura valley, its thatched Shariden reliquary hall a designated National Treasure.
Zeniarai Benzaiten Shrine
Hidden through a rock tunnel, this cave-shrine invites visitors to wash money in sacred spring water said to multiply their fortunes.
Meigetsu-in Temple (Hydrangea Temple)
In June thousands of blue hydrangeas engulf this Zen temple, whose famous round window frames a perfect living picture of the inner garden.
Komachi-dōri Street
A cheerful pedestrian lane from the station to the great shrine, packed with snack stalls, craft shops and purple-sweet-potato ice cream.
Enoshima Island and the Enoden Railway
The retro Enoden tram hugs the coast to this shrine-topped island of caves, sea candles and, on clear days, Mount Fuji silhouettes.

train.note: Japan has no international trains, and Kamakura is really a day trip from Tokyo rather than a long-distance destination. The fastest way in is the JR Yokosuka Line, about an hour from Tokyo Station for Y920 or 25 minutes from Yokohama for Y330; Shonan-Shinjuku Line trains also run through from Shinjuku. A prettier alternative is the Odakyu line from Shinjuku to Fujisawa and then the rattling Enoden tram-train along the coast past Enoshima into Kamakura, roughly 90 minutes in total. Odakyu's Enoshima-Kamakura Free Pass covers that return trip plus unlimited Enoden rides for a day and is usually the best value.

bus.note: There are no international buses from Japan, and Kamakura has no long-distance coach terminal - intercity buses use Yokohama or Tokyo instead, from where the train is faster anyway. Local Enoden Bus and Keikyu Bus services radiate from the east exit of Kamakura Station to Hase, Kita-Kamakura and the temple valleys, paid by IC card on board. If you are arriving on an overnight coach from western Japan, Willer Express (https://willerexpress.com/en/) and other operators drop at Yokohama, about 25 minutes away by JR.

ferry.note: Kamakura faces Sagami Bay but has no scheduled passenger ferry or commuter boat service. The only local boats are seasonal sightseeing cruises around Enoshima, a few kilometres west along the Enoden line, and they run on fine days only.

half.name: Yokohama
half.blurb: Japan's second-largest city has a historic Chinatown, a harbor-front park, and a red-brick warehouse district converted into shops and restaurants.

half.name: Odawara Castle
half.blurb: A reconstructed feudal-era castle with a museum and keep overlooks Sagami Bay, once a key checkpoint on the old Tokaido road.

half.name: Hakone
half.blurb: A mountain resort town known for hot spring baths, a ropeway over volcanic vents, and views of Mount Fuji across Lake Ashi.
